newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: BP sees crude output up, faces rebel threat.
newsitem.headline: BP sees crude output up, faces rebel threat.

text.p: Oil output at British Petroleum-operated Cusiana oil field in Colombia's eastern plains will rise to between 250,000 and 300,000 barrels per day within the next two months, a company spokesman said Tuesday.

Meanwhile, threats by leftist rebels against BP's facilities at the nearby Cupiagua field, which is not due to come on stream until early 1998, have caused the company between $7 million and $10 million in losses in the last two-and-a-half weeks, the spokesman said.

A Bogota-based BP spokesman said work on expanding facilities at the Cusinana field was being completed, and crude output would rise from current levels of about 185,000 barrels per day to a maximum of about 300,000 bpd by late July or early August.
But in the sister field of Cupiagua, which like Cusiana is operated by BP in association with state-run oil company Ecopetrol, Total and Triton Energy Corp, work has virtually ground to a halt.

Guerrillas of the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest rebel force, broadcast threats against the foreign oil companies and their contract workers via a local radio station two-and-a-half weeks ago.

Since then, ELN has seized and burned five buses transporting contract workers to the field and a small bomb exploded at one of the contractors offices in the regional center of Yopal about two weeks ago.

Last week contracts with four main contractors, 25 subcontractors and an estimated 1,000 workers were suspended. But the BP spokesman said those contracts were formally severed Tuesday and will only be renewed once the contractors decide it is safe to resume work.

The threats have halted the drilling of four wells and two flow lines which coupled with standby payments to workers and security and administrative costs have meant losses of between $7 million and $10 million for BP.
"It is too early to say whther these threats will affect development at Cupiagua. We will only know that at the start of next year," the BP official said.
"Operations at Cusinana, however, remain completely normal and have not been affected," he added.
Security at BP's fields is largely the responsibility of the Colombian government and its armed forces.
BP, Triton and Total agreed to pay the armed forces, via the Finance Ministry, $9 million over three years which under the terms of the accord is destined for non-lethal material.

In an interview with daily El Tiempo over the weekend, Ecopetrol chief Antonio Urdinola warned Casanare province, where BP operations are centered, was gripped by conflict between leftist rebels and right-wing paramilitary groups.
He accused the ELN of trying to blackmail the oil companies to raise funds to fill their war chests.
